utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Although my court agenda and procedural issues have been grown over the weekend considerably, I'll limit myself to only one of them and that is to put on the record the communication with the parties about the funding matter, funding for assistance of an expert. It's of such importance that it's -- was sent on the 11th of December by e-mail to the parties and reads as follows: "Dear parties, "On 7th December 2015, in its tenth report on Tomasica experts, the Defence requested that the Chamber direct the Registry to provide funding for the travel, accommodation, and work of two of witness Radovanovic's assistants in relation to a scheduled trip to The Hague in late December 2015. The Chamber understands that the Defence is seeking judicial review of the Registrar's decision to deny the request for these funds. "On 10th of December, the Registry opposed the Defence's 7th of December request, arguing that the Chamber is not competent to decide the matter and that the usual practice is to use the lump sum for these expenses. "Article 31 of the Directive on Assignment of Defence Counsel deals with the settlement of disputes over payment. Generally, if the applicable provisions do not provide a basis for judicial review of an administrative decision, the statutory obligations of a Chamber to ensure a fair trial provides such a basis. Article 31(C) provides for review by the President for disputes involving a sum greater than €4,999. The Defence has not specified the amount at issue, and therefore the Chamber cannot determine whether the correct forum for judicial review is the President or itself. However, even if the Chamber was the correct forum, the Defence has not submitted the relevant Registry decision to be reviewed, nor has it presented any arguments towards fulfilling its onus of persuasion in this regard. "Accordingly, the Chamber denies the Defence's request. "Lastly the Chamber notes that the Registry's decision denying the funds at issue was seemingly issued in July 2015. The issue was also raised in court in August 2015, but the Defence never requested the Chamber's intervention until the 7th of December. The Chamber strongly urges the Defence to avoid any further delays in this matter. If the travel of the two assistants is indispensable for the Defence case, the Defence should seriously consider arranging this travel as scheduled and pay for the expense from its lump sum for now. Any reimbursement can then still be sought without further delaying the drafting of witness Radovanovic's report. "This decision will be placed on the record in due course." Well, this last line now is hereby fulfilled. Before we ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, Mr. Lukic, we received notice that you said I think that you'd need at least four and a half hours in light of the Chamber's guidance. This surprises us, to some extent, because the main issue of the guidance was that much of what is found in the report is beyond the scope of the expertise of the witness. So we would can be rather expect a reduction in time of dealing with the witness. Because spending more time on issues which still are not within the scope of the expertise is not what the Chamber expects you to do. I leave it to that. We'll see how you develop, but please keep in mind that that was the main issue in our guidance, and the sources matter was in addition to that but not replacing our concerns about the witness telling all kind of things which are really not within his expertise. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, I'm going to ask you something about the Institute For Missing Persons first. Why was it established and what is its purpose?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The Institute for Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established by Bosnia-Herzegovina, actually due to the obligation that Bosnia-Herzegovina took upon itself within the General Framework Agreement signed in Dayton. And it says, inter alia, that it will ensure the right of the families of missing persons to find out what the fate of their family members was. This is an international agreement that was signed about the founders, the role of founders, of the Institute for Missing Persons. This was signed by the International Commission for missing persons, ICMP, and the Council of Ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you work in the Institute for Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From when until when?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I worked there from the beginning of April 2009 until sometime in the month of October 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. What are the basic legal frameworks within which the institute functions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, this is the Law on Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the agreement that I've already referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is defined in the agreement? What are the powers of the institute?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Article 4 of the mentioned agreement, inter alia, states that the responsibilities of the Institute are the collection and processing of information, all information about missing persons, locations of individual and mass graves, the establishment of central records of missing persons. Then, further on, finding, verifying and marking locations of individual and mass graves, participation in exhumations, participation in sanitisation, in autopsies, anthropological examinations of mortal remains, on-site investigations, the establishment of co-operation with judiciary institutions, and all other local and international institutions and organisations that are relevant to the quest for missing persons, including the institution that we are in today. These are some of the responsibilities of the institute defined in this international agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We haven't had this in the system so I cannot show it to you, but I will show you now 1D05450. We'll take a look at the law. So what we have before us is the Law on Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 2 in both version, B/C/S and English, first Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So please tell us what it says. Could you clarify this for us? We see what is written here.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this article speaks of the responsibility of Bosnia-Herzegovina - the obligation of Bosnia-Herzegovina - and that is defined in this law. That is the right of missing persons' family members to learn the fate of their missing family members and relatives; and if it is established that such a person is still living, then we are supposed to provide the family members with information concerning the residence of the said person. However, if it established that the person is no longer alive, then the families should be provided relevant information about the cause of death, the place of burial of their family member, and of course to have the mortal remains of that family member returned to them if they were identified in the first place. So that is the basic task of the Institute for Missing Persons. Now, if you wish, I can give you a comment --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we see Article 4.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The obligation to secure information.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see what is written here, but what is the gist of this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This article of the Law on Missing Persons is important because it provides a legal basis for our work, wherein all institutions and organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including defence legislation, internal affairs and all the others are under obligation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, is there any dispute about that's a proper legal basis for the institute to work, to do its job?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's crucial for us to show what this gentleman's work was, work in which field --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you are showing at this moment is what the law says --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

So would you please focus on what is the issue rather than to establish the underlying legislation which is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have before us Article 5.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says: "The competent authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are duty-bound, based on earlier and recent applications for available information, to trace and verify all the available information, citing all the sources that have been checked in identifying such information in relation to the disappearance of the subject of the search," et cetera. What does it look like on the ground? What was your job at the Institute for tracing missing persons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The first 14 months I worked as a senior assistant in the commission for verification of information about missing persons; and then four months [as interpreted] as head of sector for searching for missing persons and identifying missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have on record that you were head of sector for four months.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was close to four and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see a reference here to new information from the ground. Where are you looking for new information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in keeping with the articles of the law we've just seen, all institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina are under obligation to provide, at our request, all the relevant information to the Institute for Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina because the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina transferred the responsibility for the whole process of tracing missing persons on to us, as stipulated in Article 30 of this law, which states that the Law on Missing Persons has priority over all the other laws in Bosnia-Herzegovina where missing persons are concerned, that is, a framework. Now when we're talking about the sector for tracing exhumations and identifications that I headed, I can also explain about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do allow me to put a question to the witness for clarification. You said you were head of sector for searching for missing persons and identifying missing persons. How many people worked in this sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in that sector, I had five district and regional offices and a total of 30 employees out of a total of 52 total employed in the Institute for Missing Persons.

All this information came to my desk and I processed it, analysed it, sorted it across lower levels in my sector, moving it to their desks, following up on their work, managing their work, and also, because we investigated every case individually, I established co-operation with all the relevant institutions, domestic and international, judicial, prosecutorial, intelligence, police, military, international organisations such as the ICMP, the ICRC, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

"Carries out technical and other work related to the tracing, collection, and processing of applications, statements, and information on missing persons, on individual and mass graves." Here I would like to dwell more on the processing of applications. It says that this is one of your tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry. It says: [Interpretation] Statements, processing of statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What type of statements did you deal with in your work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, we always tried through our operative work, both on the ground and through the institutional approach specified by the law, we tried to procure information from institutions that we considered relevant because the missing persons we were looking for went missing in the war, so the most important documents for us are military documents, statements from security organs, military and public security. We're talking about people who testified about events. We're talking about security analyses that in -- security organs supplied to higher levels. Those were primary documents. But when we are talking about the work of operative officers in our sector, they also took statements from certain witnesses or from the families, depending on what information was available to whom, or through their network of sources on the ground they received information because we are under obligation to keep the confidentiality of sources they provided this information to me, they submitted it to me. That is the framework and range of documents that we dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since there is no translation, I will just say for the record, it says: "Carries out investigations and other work related to missing persons."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge also asked you what does that mean? How do you do that research and investigation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As I've said, my position as head of sector is the position actually of the first operative officer in Bosnia-Herzegovina as far as missing persons are concerned. My people in that sector, after receiving information from the family that a family member is missing, our employee first checks through our records whether that person is alive. When it's established whether the person is alive or not, as I've said before, if the person is alive, we look for information about their whereabouts. If not, we proceed with a classical investigation. We gather all the available documentation in order to put together a mosaic about the circumstances in which the person went missing, to reconstruct the event from a security/intelligence point of view, to try to trace the person and see where it ended up. The input information is what the family reported, such as the place where the person went missing. This is the first input that is, for the most part, not correct because the question asked of the families is: Where did you see the family member alive for the last time? Answer -- the answer may not be correct because the person could have gone missing hundreds of kilometres away from where they were last seen, as we had one case where in Rijeka 1999 was the place where the person was last seen and we exhumed that person in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 2012 or 2013, a long way away from where they were last seen. That is our last part of the job --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, may I ask you a question. If you ask someone: Where was he last seen? And he says it was at home or in my village and he's exhumed 200 kilometres further away, what is not correct in that answer? That answer is fully correct, it seems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is correct. However, the information provided is not, that the person lost his or her life there and then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but if that is not asked, then of course you couldn't expect the answer to say something which is not asked. So the answer, I now do understand, is correct and you made a mistake when you say when you ask where he was seen last, they say at home, that that is not correct. That is -- that is in itself not correct, although it gives us any clues as to where that person died and it doesn't give any clue as to where that person was buried. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in principle, it's not that simple because certain families in some cases have more information and others have less. That is important for our operative work. We double-check the information that the family provided so that we can trace the person if the assumption is that the person is deceased. So I'm talking about operative work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're moving away from my question. That the operative work includes more is perfectly clear. Mr. Lukic, the inaccuracy of the information often given by families has been dealt with in quite some detail over the last two years and that's clear. Often family members do not know where their loved one died or were exhumed, and that seems not to be in dispute -- at least I never heard of any dispute about that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was an answer to your question. I didn't try to clarify that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us now, in practice you asked the prosecutor's office for information, you asked the court for information, the military intelligence organisation or state security. Can they refuse to provide information to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: According to the Law on Missing Persons, in Article 30 of that law everybody is duty-bound, including the institutions that you mentioned, to provide the information that we need for our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer 1D06333 into evidence and we will probably make very short selection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it that you want it to be MFI'd for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: MFI, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D1375, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Witness, when you were asked whether courts -- the court should give information, which court did you understand to be covered by this question? Would that include the ICTY, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it pertains to institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We can look at the relevant provisions of the law in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't to do that but that was "the court," where there are many courts in this world. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I have a follow-up question. Sorry for that. With respect to the question person last seen somewhere by whom, when, do you see any differences in the way to proceed between your work and the work of the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The International Commission, ICMP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The International Committee for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I explained the mandate of the institute as briefly as possible but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that is not my question. Please focus on my question. Do you see any difference in the way to proceed to establish place and date of death in the work of the ICMP and your institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I wished to give you an answer, but I will try to do it now. There is a fundamental difference and if you wish I can expand on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If this would not disturb your line of questioning, Mr. Lukic, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mandate and responsibilities of the ICMP involve collecting blood samples and bone samples from post-mortems and exhumations in order to carry out DNA analysis assisting in sanitisation, speaking of skeletal remains, because they have anthropologists too. They do not have the responsibility or mechanisms to carry out the investigations that we carry out. There can be no comparison in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But what is the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They cannot establish the circumstances of death. They cannot provide response to families. They don't have the mechanism to do that; and according to law, that is what we do. They take blood samples, they take bone samples, and then when taking blood samples from family members, then they get information on when the said persons were last seen and then they provide technical assistance to us, and that's it. The main body of our work is collecting information and intelligence and documentation in order to put together this mosaic and to see where the person was, where the person died, whether the person was thrown into a pit, a river, whatever. So basically this comes as the very end of our huge efforts to put together this picture, how persons went missing. As I've already told you, many imprisoned persons were hidden and then killed. Many persons were relocated. And it is an enormous problem for us to create this reconstruction, to create this mosaic, if you will, in terms of how these persons went missing. Exhumation and identification are the easiest part of the job. It's not important. I mean, I'm not saying it's not important, but I'm saying that it's a lot less than this other part of our work that I told you about. I hope that this will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. I think it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for a break. We'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minute, Mr. Pavlovic. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it was announced that you would have a matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. And good morning, Your Honours and everyone in the courtroom. I wanted to return to a brief discussion we had last -- at the end of last week concerning the words limits for the final trial briefs, and this may be a useful point, it may be a pedantic point, but I thought it best to raise it so that we're indeed all on the same page, as it were. When I mentioned the number of words in the final brief that had been -- on which we had a consensus view between the parties, the Chamber asked whether in terms of the number of pages, 300.000 words you know were -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can tell you, I meanwhile verified that the standard page is 300 words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's it, exactly. Thank you, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry to come about it less directly and you were obviously on top of it, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we considered that, because I think I gave an estimate which was rather based on 400 words a page. But our standard page, especially with the space between the lines, et cetera, comes down to 300 pages, but -- well, you may have noticed that we -- 300 words a page, and we have -- we are considering it on that basis at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We talked about methodology and now I'd like to show you document 1D06201; that's your CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need page 3 in B/C/S -- sorry, page 4 in B/C/S, page 3 in English. We have to go one page back in English. Yeah, second page. Our system was shortly not working again, so we were not able to check correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last reference here is that from October 2009 -- from April 2009 until October 2014, you were working at the BiH Missing Persons Institute as head of the tracing, exhumation, and identification sector of the central records of missing persons, so that's about four years. Is that your last job, the one that you revved to here, until 2014, October?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. From October 2014, I became employed at the Republican Centre for War Crimes and for Seeking Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we deal with that, is -- Do you have any military experience? Did you serve in the army? Did you get any military training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I first note that there is a mistranslation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, you have developed a habit of first making all kind of observations. We'd very much like you, first of all, to answer the question. And then if there's any mistake to be corrected, then you have an opportunity to do so. But could you first answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hmm. Thank you for this explanation. As for military experience, I did my regular military service in the JNA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for a short while. And afterwards, it was established that, due to certain problems - claustrophobia, so on and so forth, I was returned because the assessment was that a couple of years later I could be checked again so that it would be established whether I could continue my military service. I'm sorry, what was the other question you had for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you had any military training. But could you first now tell us then how long you had been in the army. You said it was a short period of time. For how long were you in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the regular military service, and I was there, say, for about 40 days or 45 days. I was in the quartermaster's corps, and I had standard military training of a general nature. I cannot define it now exactly, how different it was in relation to the other branches and services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you had no other military training than what you obtained in those 40 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. I mean, nothing formal or of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You tendered the document. The CV of the witness, Mr. Registrar would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D06201 will be Exhibit D1376, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see on our screens the next document, it's 1D06202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we still not have an English translation of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's 1D06332.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We addressed the Republican Institute for Investigating War Crimes and Finding Missing Persons so we could get an explanation of the work that you carry out today. There is a document here. In the last paragraph on this page in both versions, it says that you take part in collecting statements, other documents and data relevant for the department; you review and analyse documents relevant for the department; take part in pre-visits to sites. It also says, up here, that you are senior associate for exhumation, forensic processing, identification, records, and field-work in the processing of searching for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now need the next page in both versions. The second paragraph in the English version, and in B/C/S it says: "Besides these duties and according to his previous experience as the head of the Department for Search, Exhumation and Identification in the Institute of Missing Persons of the BiH, operational position number 1 in BH related to missing persons, Mr. Pavlovic, since October 2014, had been responsible for the analysis of the events in and around Srebrenica in July 1995." Further down, it says: "The tasks of Mr. Pavlovic are the following: Documenting and analysing the fate of the bodies of persons who lost their lives in the breakthrough towards the territory controlled by BiH army, documenting and analysing their identities, and analysing lists of persons recorded as missing related to the events in Srebrenica in July 1995." Could you please tell us now, in practice, what is your work look like? What do you do.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to a large part, methodologically it does not differ from my previous work in the Institute for Missing Persons, but now I am involved in the work that you mentioned and, in fact, I deal with a narrow particular event. The methodology of work does not basically change. All possible documentation from that period is collected: Military, intelligence, police, witness statements. This is dealt with analytically, it is sorted out, certain conclusions are reached, and then they are verified on the ground. So that would be it in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may ask a question for clarification. Sir, are you able to show us in your report where you analyse the identities of the people that you wrote about in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the analysis that I submitted here, there are such passages -- I would have to go through the analysis now to find them, but they are definitely there, because I followed the path of the column to understand what happened during that breakthrough, the persons who lost their lives during the breakthrough, where they were killed, where they were later found, their identifies. Not in a large measure, only within the limits of the task I was given, when charged with drafting this analysis. But if I had been asked to, I could have provided a list of the people who were killed during the breakthrough. But I already opened up a tool that enables very quickly to list a certain number of persons, and I have an attachment to this analysis listing 600 or more identities of such persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I probably may have received an incomplete report. I just want you to point us in your report to where you analyse the identities, and you can tell us this -- these remains belong to X because of this kind of identification process that I have gone through. It may very well be that my report -- the one I got, is incomplete. I'm just asking you to point us to that portion in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this analysis also has more than 100 attachments, including excerpts from books and documents, and my contribution is a list with those identities. Now I don't know how to provide it to you, but it's part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can give the 65 ter number, Your Honour, if you want so we can see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have on our screens 1D06331, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I take it this was contained in the latest list of documents to be used with this witness not in the first one --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not in the first one --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not the first one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- when you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- you are right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- not at that time when you provided us with the report itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We didn't have it, so we couldn't upload it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's been my problem when I prepared for this witness because I just didn't have this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not sure, Your Honour. We didn't have this document with us, it's overview, and we anticipated that it -- that kind of questions could arise and Mr. Pavlovic kindly provided this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess it would have been helpful if we had been pre-warned that there's still part that's going to come, because we've been looking for this kinds of information and I couldn't find it anywhere. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One second, I check where we were before this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before you do so, Mr. Lukic, is there any explanation why -- as to why the last employment of the witness doesn't appear on his CV? I mean, you asked us to -- to decide on expertise, et cetera, and then what now turns out perhaps to be a relevant part - I don't know yet - is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document was that was actually provided by republican Ministry of Justice was attached with the response to the Prosecution -- to Prosecution's filing on this qualification of this witness so it was available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if the witness works there for a year now, wouldn't it be your duty to add to the CV relevant information about his present employment, rather than to wait for -- I mean, I would have expected that so that we have a better basis it decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's an omission on our side, Your Honour, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it would cure the flaws described is a different matter, but at least we would like to have had complete information. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would offer this, 1D06332, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see what it is. Yes. I now see that that's overview of known individuals who died --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thought the previous document. I will be dealing with this document later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the previous document. No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Not to the CV, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, I know that not everyone in Scotland is called MacGregor, that's -- I apologise for that. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1377, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. I think I earlier did not call your name exactly, that's -- apologies for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's cast our minds back to the institute for tracing missing persons. Who works for you as the head of sector in that institute, which profile of people on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who works for you at the institute for tracing missing persons, which profile of employee works for you as the head of sector?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: My work colleagues from the sector with whom I had the honour of working come from all ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They are former members of the state security, military security, public security, who worked as inspectors for general crime, violent crimes, war crimes, colleagues who have worked as scene-of-crime officers who are able to do the foot work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are there some who were involved in exchanges during the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are some who worked in the army and dealt with exchanges of both living persons and bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to turn to your report. We are not going to deal with the first 20 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, that is to say, the first 18. In B/C/S, in keeping with the instructions of the Court, we are not going to rely on that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So would you please turn to page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the screen, we would need 1D06200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which is D1373, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When this column was moving, what are the main locations where losses were incurred?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In the first part of the movement of the column, I mean until the crossing of the road from Konjevic Polje to Nova Kasaba, there are three main locations of conflict and death, that is to say, losses of the 28th Division. Then during the crossing of the road. And then, in the second part of the breakthrough, there are perhaps three other main locations, but throughout the breakthrough the 28th Division was under artillery fire and infantry fire, and one can say that losses were sustained in the whole length of the breakthrough, according to statements and testimonies of eye-witnesses. The column was under fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly which witnesses and what statements? Do we have these statements? Do we not have them? Could you give us the details of what your conclusions are based upon, irrespective of whether it's for you to make such conclusions, but at least that we know what it is that you considered when telling us this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I was replying to the specific question put to me, but this analysis cites witness statements with details about what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the material you relied upon, is that found in the footnotes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And some parts of that material are quoted in the body of the analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know - or does Mr. Lukic know - whether some of these statements, for example, whether they are in evidence before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that we do have some already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some. But has it systematically been analysed? What is before us? Because if this witness draws conclusions on the basis of statements which are not known to us, we cannot verify whether we would draw similar conclusions because it is finally for the Chamber to decide what happened not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will offer those statements into evidence. It will be in our evidence after -- or during the testimony of this witness. That was our intention exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then leave the conclusions to us rather than to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, you will be the final judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Another question is: Did you consult any material apart from what you footnoted, statements which are not footnoted, for example, or documents which are not footnoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. There were other documents that I reviewed that, for many reasons, I did not cite in the analysis itself either because I tried to keep this paper to a certain length or because I found some documents later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now start from 12 July 1995. Do you know where Buljim is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you describe briefly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, briefly, it's on the road from which the 28th Division set out to try to break out of the encirclement from Susnjari and Jaglici. That is essentially where the lines held by both armies were located and there at Buljim, Ravni Buljim, members of the 28th Division entered the territory controlled by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see 1D06235 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll soon see before us the statement of Nedzad Ademovic given to the State Security Service in Tuzla on 7th August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think we have a translation yet. That is the statement we need, page 2, please, paragraphs 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the name of this witness again, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, his name is - one second, I moved to another page - is Nedzad Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that footnote -- let's have a look?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's footnote 51A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the middle of the screen, it says: "The 284th Brigade set out immediately." And in the next paragraph, it says: "The Chetniks opened fire on us from artillery and infantry weapons. I passed through the first ambush and did not notice how many fighters got killed or wounded. The attack lasted for about 20 minutes but since there were so many of us, almost every bullet fired would kill one fighter of ours." In this part of this statement, we do not see how many persons were killed. Why is this statement important to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you are stating in your report that what is ascribed to crime is exaggerated and is not in accordance with the truth and is even, for political reasons, put at a certain point in time before the public, et cetera. I have the following question for you. If you say -- and I'm just -- this is a hypothesis just. Let's just assume that it's reported that 10.000 people are missing. If you, for example, would say, Well, in the column 8.000 must have died - I'm not saying that you are telling us this - and if we have other evidence which says, for example, 5.000 people were killed. Then I have 13.000 people which are dead, whereas 10.000 are reported to be missing. How, in your view, could we establish whether either the 5.000 killed by crime is too large, or whether the assessment of 8.000 being killed in the column is too big? Because the two together give us more dead people than are reported missing. Do you have any -- I mean, you focussed very much on the one. You didn't deal with the prisoners of war. Others have done so. And if those two collide, what's -- what should -- what should we do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quite understand the point of your question, and that's a very good question. My job was to take into account all the documents, statements, and analyses available to me, and based on that - as an expert and a man with experience in that job - estimate what could be realistic numbers and losses. I believe my documents are similar or the same as those used by the Defence so far. I cannot estimate whether a person gave a security organ correct information. It's the courts, the judicial and investigative authorities, whose responsibility it is to take statements and to establish which people got killed during the breakthrough and which were killed in different ways name by name. I am presenting my conclusions as an expert and it is up to you, of course, the Court, to judge what is what. That is my humble opinion, and I hope I have been of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This statement that you have commented upon so far that we've reviewed, did they refer to executions or to losses sustained during the movement of the column?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you a 100 per cent exact answer, but I know that there are statements among these that refer to different ways of death, and you can probably find it in the statements attached to the report and footnoted. But in view of my particular task, I dealt with one part only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The numbers we've cited here, does it only include what the witnesses referred to as losses sustained during the movement of the column, or that number given, for instance, by the last witness, an OTP investigator? Would it include people who were executed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that from the knowledge we gained from the documents and statements as to what happened in that area in that specific place, my supposition and my conclusion is that the greatest majority of persons whose bodies were found there got killed in the fighting between the two sides, in internal fighting, suicides, et cetera, because panic reigned in that column and, unfortunately, they also shot at one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just for clarity, the Prosecution position is certainly there were a large number of people who were prisoners of war and executed, but also that some -- some people in the column surrendered and were executed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And I wonder if my friend could just distinguish between them when he asks his questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it's self-explanatory from the statements about which victims these witnesses are testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Lot of survivors couldn't have been victims of murders. That's for sure. We only have a few, I think, witnesses who have stated that they survived mass executions, but I think that those who gave statements to the -- Tuzla they -- I think what we've seen until now are mainly stating about what happened in the column, irrespective of whether it's always accurate or reliable, credible - that's still to be tested - but that seems to be what Mr. Lukic is presenting and you have any doubt as to whether there's any confusion in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It was just, Your Honour, with regard to Your Honour's question about what Mr. Pavlovic's role was, what his task was, and he said he was excluding the number of people who had been executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The Prosecution position is that some people who were in the column were also executed. They're not in the mass graves necessarily but that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you mean there were executions in the column as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you keep that in the back of your mind, so as to clearly distinguish -- Meanwhile, I think we should first take a break, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll -- you may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I think after the present witness we have one more witness to go. There is no way this week that we could have extended sessions for practical reasons. It's -- therefore, the parties are urged to conclude the evidence of those two witnesses, because the next witness, I think, is scheduled for two hours in-chief, two hours cross. And with this witness, I think we should be able to conclude in such a time that there will be sufficient time left for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I just wanted to put this on the record that we are not left with half an hour or one or two hours which would then have to be postponed until early February and then travelling twice, et cetera. We should try to complete our programme this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to finish this witness as well, Your Honour. Although I clarified with Mr. Pavlovic he told me that, if necessary, he would come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you say? You will not finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will do my best to finish this witness and I do want to finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- his examination this week, but I said that I clarified with Mr. Pavlovic - and he's listening now - that's he's willing even to come back if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we will try to avoid that in any case --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think we have, apart from this now short session, we have three days left, for which -- we would have two days for this witness. And I'm also looking at you, Mr. MacDonald. Your time for cross was scheduled at?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Our current estimate is two hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can, sorry, just add quickly. Given that we weren't sure what my friend was going to go out in-chief, we may ask for some leeway but right now we don't see it going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we'll start with the next witness anyway tomorrow morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but then we would continue on Wednesday. And there's no way that we could not conclude the evidence of two witness this week. It's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm pretty confident that we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's good, Mr. Lukic. That's very good that you are confident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope that the Prosecution would hurry up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand you, which is not the same as I agree with you. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have 1D06265, please. It's 55L -- J footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see soon a statement dated 14 September 1995. [In English] Again, yeah on this one it is visible it is composed on this day on the first line. First line of the text there is a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 14th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is it the same witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- as the witness on the footnote? Is this Alija Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's -- that top part is probably from the previous statement. That's the format where you have something from previous statements, but the record is that you have the second paragraph where you have the name of this witness, Mujanovic, Isad. It says [B/C/S spoken] Mujanovic, Isad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We need page 2 and we'll look at the line 3 from the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says -- because we have no translation I'll read this short passage that we need: "The column in which I ran into the first ambush got to Kamenica where fire was opened upon us from all possible artillery and other weapons, and there, in my estimate, from what I saw, around 1.000 persons were killed. At that time, we picked up and carried the wounded, and then when we ran into new ambushes, we dropped them because everyone ran for their lives." Mr. Pavlovic, in other statements as well, did you come across information that the wounded were left behind, that the unwounded members did not go on carrying them -- excuse me, just a moment my colleague has an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was waiting for you to finish the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Just to say that we do object, Your Honour. It's a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly is, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Quite apart from now leading evidence that is not here. You were to ask about this one, not in other statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, please, rephrase your question or put another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then I'll ask the witness, the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you able to determine reading this statement the place where this happened? Which situation is this person describing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This witness also describes the events at Kamenica near Bratunac, just under Sandici and Kravica. But he says that in his part of the column, he ran into the first ambush at Kamenica, where around 1.000 persons were killed that he saw. And he later says that he cannot put a number on all the dead bodies and the wounded people he saw at that time. Speaking about the number of the wounded in such situations where the 28th Division was fighting against the other side, it frequently happened that the wounded were left behind by their fellow fighters who were longer able to carry them. In some other statement, I was able to see the people who saw certain fellow fighters wounded, when they returned to the same place, they saw that the wounded had succumbed to their wounds. So regrettably a certain number of the wounded could not be saved. They died.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand this statement is also unsigned, so we wonder if it could be MFI'd until we check the provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statement is unsigned and without translation. Mr. Registrar, the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D06265 will be MFI D1386, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. I'm wondering, Mr. Lukic, is there no way to -- I mean, the Prosecution has presented its evidence. You want to present statements saying that the numbers of those who were killed in the column might be large or at least that the statements give their number there, mainly assessments, rather rough assessments. But why not find a way to have that in evidence? These, of course, are statements of witnesses who did not appear. At the same time, the statements were not taken for Tribunal purposes and in that respect are not covered by Rule 92 bis. Why not -- because what happens now is that the witness draws all kinds of conclusions on the basis of this limited materials which, of course, doesn't assist us greatly because that's -- these materials -- whereas this Chamber has to look at all the materials before it, and that could include these ones. But is there not another way to say, Well, that's what the witness stated in Tuzla in 1995 and then we'll have to -- I mean, this witness can't help us very much in weighing that evidence. He -- I don't know, it seems that he was not present when these statements were taken, but he draws conclusions on the basis of it, whereas -- well, I've said already before, it doesn't help in that respect that he may emphasise more these than others which he may not even be aware of. Is there not a practical way of dealing with this matter without spending hours and hours in court to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have 20 more minutes and maybe after the court sitting I can meet with the Prosecution, and if they have any proposition we are open to discuss it with him. But, as I told you before, in this regard the burden of proof was switched to the Defence because the Prosecution never investigated -- never investigated this, although their investigators were aware. We read Mr. Ruez's statement to him today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- stay away from whether the Prosecution -- I'm at this moment pointing at the matter which, whether or not it was investigated or not by them is not something -- you now put your evidence before us and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At least we do not have any evidence on that, because our materials do not show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that it's investigated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are already starting with the evaluation of the evidence which is before us and that's for the Chamber to do at later stage. I'm trying at this moment to see whether there are more practical ways of having these statements in. And then, of course, to be given its weight in the totality of the evidence with all the limitations that we haven't heard those witnesses. Mr. MacDonald, I saw Mr. McCloskey's body language seemed to be very much opposing any such solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Given that this is a rather important policy decision, we, of course, will try to reach some agreement with Mr. Lukic. However, as you can see, we haven't been really objecting to these materials coming in, and -- but we do, as you might imagine, greatly contest the accuracy. As you yourself have pointed out, there's high numbers and low numbers this is really -- that particular issue is not going to be open for discussion, but letting the material in we've been open to so that the Court can give it whatever weight it deems necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could the parties please discuss this after -- because if we proceed in this slow pace, at the end it may be that all it -- all these materials are in evidence anyhow, and then, of course, it's for us what to do with them, that is, to make them part of our evaluation. And if that can be done in a more -- in a quicker way -- and, of course, without this witness drawing conclusions on the basis of mainly these materials. And that's, of course, what is trigging me to make such an observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Some 55 witnesses that went through the woods that suffered what they sufficient and all the statements related to that, I'm not -- I don't -- it's the Prosecution position this is not going to be overly probative for you. You have seen witnesses that have testified that went through this, that were open for cross-examination. But 55 statements like this you can see from the witness's testimony, this -- this is taking us pretty far afield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A selection perhaps or an agreement between the parties that there are another 40 with numbers going from -- on the same event from 200 to 500 or 300, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem, of course, is conclusions to be drawn from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but if you could be clear on what you do or do not contest as far as existence of statements, that might help already because then the Chamber is aware that the parties do not disagree on the existence of statements with these numbers in this context, apart from what conclusions are to be drawn from that. The parties are invited to see whether they can speed up matters and reach a result which is similar to the slow pace in which we're doing it now. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on to one document I cannot introduce in evidence but I would like to see it on the screen. It's 1D00990. It's the testimony of Gavric, Mico. 55M. We need e-court page 52, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have used this transcript and you have reviewed it also for our case. From line 7 down, the witness says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think first you should introduce this document. We see it's a transcript from this Tribunal. We have no idea from which case, when that interview -- when this testimony was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This testimony is from Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 3rd of May, 2004, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I quote: "At the same time I backtracked and remembered what had happened some 20 years previously when I, going from the village of Kamenica down to Konjevic Polje, that I could have passed that route without stepping on the ground. I stepped on one body after another. So anybody who had been there would know just how many corpses there were." [Interpretation] I'm afraid of formulating my question in the wrong way. Do you know who Mico Gavric is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've had the opportunity to meet that gentleman and talk to him as part of the work I'm doing now on this subject because I have seen this transcript and I asked him what it was about, and he explained to me that as a young soldier he had occasion to talk to a well-known general, Petar Gracanin, about the battle of the Sutjeska, the scene where one could not put one's foot on the ground there were so many dead and wounded. And he compared it to this situation on the 17th of July when they were clearing the terrain going towards Kravica. And the road from Konjevic Polje to Nova Kasaba, he said it was 6 to 10 kilometres that they cleared, and he had seen a horrible scene, unimaginable to a normal person. There were so many bodies strewn on the ground where the 28th Division's column was passing. For the type of work that I am doing, it is very significant. And in view of the experience we've had, it's important to me to be able to assess the importance and the truthfulness of the statements I'm dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document now that is not a statement. It's 1D06269. It's the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 2nd Corps Command, security section. The date is 23rd August 1995. Second paragraph on this first page, it says: "It is necessary to take a detailed statement for the record from Kemal Mujic and two of his fellow fighters concerning their stay in Srebrenica in the perpetration of a war crime against the Bosniak population (the figure of 2.000 to 3.000 bodies from Buljim to Konjevic Polje is referred to) by the aggressor, and forward these in two copies as soon as possible to the OSVB of the 2nd Corps."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or "GSVP." It's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this stretch from Buljim to Konjevic Polje, from what you were able to study during your work, were there any mass executions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot make any assertions concerning that. I did not find a reference in any document to any executions from Buljim to Konjevic Polje; the line of the breakout of the 28th Division. I do not know that there were any mass executions, but I cannot rule it out. I simply did not find such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, does this document reflect a wish to investigate a war crime or the incident of killing people in a column?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we see this reference to 2.000 to 3.000 bodies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Maybe a bit late, Your Honour, but that was another leading question, in the view of the Prosecution, so we object here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's even worse, Mr. Lukic. You first put a document to the witness and then you ask him about what's described in the document, but also for the content. And then, of course, by putting the document to the witness, that's already very leading. What you should do is first start asking the questions, and then if there's any question which is either supported or contradicted by the document, then you take that second step. But, I mean, that harm is done already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, in this document it says "war crime" so it is exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- what they were asking the witness in this document, so I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By just showing it to him is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: misleading him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could have asked the witness, without showing the document, the first questions that you put to him; whether he ever came across any document which refers to war crimes, and perhaps in this context, perhaps place, fine. Did you ever see anything that a war crime was committed in or this area, or do you know whether war crimes were committed and does that material tell you in what area that happened? That's the way you ask these kind of questions, in a non-leading way. But let's move on. The harm has been done. Let's get back to the question. The question was whether in your view this document reflected a wish to investigate a war crime or the incident of killing people in a column. Yes, but the question was put. Witness, could you tell us anything about your interpretation of this document? That's a more neutral way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is evident from this that the people killed and the corpses on the stretch from Buljim to Konjevic Polje, the line of breakout of the 28th Division. Why Mr. Mehmed Zrilic, colonel of security, calls it a war crime is a subject for debate. But this is not the only case where military authorities qualify this as a war crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's not open for debate what he said because that's written in his letter. Open for debate perhaps is whether that's an accurate description, yes or no. You shouldn't mix up the two. Then you have not answered the question yet, I think. If you want an answer, please, Mr. Lukic, put this or a similar question to the witness. Otherwise, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We're close to the moment where we have to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently you would prefer to continue tomorrow, and perhaps after the parties have an opportunity to discuss --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Day after tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Day after tomorrow. Yes, you are right. Witness, we'll adjourn for the day. I instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether it's testimony given today or testimony still to be given in the coming days. We'd like to see you back, I think, in view of the schedule - two hours in chief, two hours in cross - that we could ask the witness to remain available Wednesday morning. So you don't have to be available tomorrow, but we'd like to see you back on Wednesday morning. I can't promise you that we'll start right away at 9.30 to hear further evidence from you, but you're requested to remain on standby from that moment in this court-house. I've given you the instruction. Therefore, we'd like to see you back Wednesday. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Shall I leave it here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's okay that the witness keep it but you should not speak with anyone about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow morning, Tuesday, the 15th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of December, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.17 p.m.,
